Occupancy models:
simulation and fitting
::: {style="font-size: 70%;"} WILD(FISH) 8390
Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics :::
# Motivation {visibility="hidden"} ## Outline - Motivation - Simulation - Classical analysis with 'unmarked' - Bayesian analysis with 'JAGS' ## Motivation We often want to do logistic regression, but the data are subject to measurement error. Specifically, wildlife data are often fraught with false negatives (ie, the species was there but we didn't detect it). Ignoring this source of measurement error can result in misleading inferences. - Occupancy will be under-estimated - Habitat associations may be incorrect ## Accounting for detection probability ::: {style="font-size: 75%;"} The model for the state process is the same as logistic regression: $$ \begin{gather*} \mathrm{logit}(\psi_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \cdots \\ z_i \sim \mathrm{Bern}(\psi_i) \end{gather*} $$ Model for the observation process conditional on the state process: $$ \begin{gather*} \mathrm{logit}(p_{ij}) = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 x_{ij1} + \alpha_2 x_{ij2} + \cdots \\ y_{ij} \sim \mathrm{Bern}(z_i\times p_{ij}) \end{gather*} $$ - $\psi_i$ -- probability that the species occurs at site $i$ - $z_i$ -- binary presence/absence variable at site $i$ - $p_{ij}$ -- probability of detecting the species at site $i$ on occasion $j$ - $y_{ij}$ -- binary detection/non-detection data ::: ## Assumptions Assumptions of the basic single-season occupancy models: - Population closure - Occupancy state (presence/absence) constant over time - Statistical independence - Occupancy state at one site has no impact on occupancy of other sites - Detections are independent, conditional on occupancy state - Variation in $\psi$ and $p$ described by covariates # Simulation {visibility="hidden"} ## Simulation ::: {style="font-size: 75%;"} Simplest case with no covariates: - Specify the parameters and dimensions ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} psi <- 0.5 ## Occurrence probability p <- 0.2 ## Detection probability nSites <- 20 nVisits <- 4 ``` ::: - Now, simulate presence-absence ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(3439) ## Just to make it reproducible z <- rbinom(nSites, size=1, psi) ## pres/absence ``` ::: - Simulate observations ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} y <- matrix(NA, nrow=nSites, ncol=nVisits) for(i in 1:nSites) { y[] <- rbinom(nVisits, size=1, prob=z[]*p) } ``` ::: ::: ## Simulated data ::: {.columns style="font-size: 80%;"} ::: {.column width='40%'} Observations ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} y ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [1,] 0 0 0 0 [2,] 0 0 0 0 [3,] 0 0 0 0 [4,] 0 0 0 0 [5,] 0 0 0 0 [6,] 0 0 0 0 [7,] 0 0 0 0 [8,] 0 0 0 0 [9,] 0 0 0 0 [10,] 0 0 0 0 [11,] 0 0 0 0 [12,] 0 0 0 0 [13,] 0 0 0 0 [14,] 0 0 0 0 [15,] 0 0 0 0 [16,] 0 0 0 0 [17,] 0 0 0 0 [18,] 0 0 0 0 [19,] 0 0 0 0 [20,] 0 0 0 0 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width='60%'}
Summary stats
Detections at each site ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} siteDets <- rowSums(y) # Dets at each site table(siteDets) # Frequency ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` siteDets 0 20 ``` ::: ::: Proportion of sites known to be occupied ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} naiveOccupancy <- sum(siteDets>0)/nSites naiveOccupancy ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: # Model fitting ## R package 'unmarked' Install and load the package ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## install.packages("unmarked") library(unmarked) ``` ::: Documentation (help files) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} help("unmarked") ``` ::: Documentation (vignettes) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} vignette(package="unmarked") ## vignette("spp-dist") ``` ::: ## R package 'unmarked' Unlike standard model fitting functions such as `lm` and `glm` that require data to be in `data.frames`, data for `unmarked' has to be formatted in an `unmarkedFrame`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} umf <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y=y) summary(umf) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` unmarkedFrame Object 20 sites Maximum number of observations per site: 4 Mean number of observations per site: 4 Sites with at least one detection: 0 Tabulation of y observations: 0 80 ``` ::: ::: ## R package 'unmarked' Fit the single-season occupancy model ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fm <- occu(~1 ~1, umf) summary(fm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: occu(formula = ~1 ~ 1, data = umf) Occupancy (logit-scale): Estimate SE z P(>|z|) -14.6 21305 -0.000685 0.999 Detection (logit-scale): Estimate SE z P(>|z|) -7.67 21961 -0.000349 1 AIC: 4 Number of sites: 20 ``` ::: ::: Estimates obtained using maximum likelihood ## R package 'unmarked' Occupancy estimate ($\hat{\psi}$) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} backTransform(fm, type="state") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Backtransformed linear combination(s) of Occupancy estimate(s) Estimate SE LinComb (Intercept) 4.63e-07 0.00986 -14.6 1 Transformation: logistic ``` ::: ::: Detection probability estimate ($\hat{p}$) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} backTransform(fm, type="det") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Backtransformed linear combination(s) of Detection estimate(s) Estimate SE LinComb (Intercept) 0.000466 10.2 -7.67 1 Transformation: logistic ``` ::: ::: ## Two types of occupancy estimates ::: {style="font-size: 70%;"} Unconditional occupancy $\psi=\Pr(z=1)$ - The estimate $\hat{\psi}$ that we computed earlier can be thought of as a prediction that we could use for a new site or a new time period Conditional occupancy $\psi^* = \Pr(z_i=1|y_{i})$ - Conditional occupancy estimates only apply to sites in the sample, at the time of sampling - In 'unmarked', conditional occupancy is computed using Empirical Bayes methods, with the `ranef` and `bup` functions. In JAGS, full Bayesian inference is used instead. - Conditional occupancy estimates can be used to answer questions like: * Which sites were occupied? * How many sites were occupied? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Posterior probs Pr(z_i=1 | y_i) z.post <- ranef(fm) ## Extract posterior means psi.conditional <- bup(z.post, stat="mean") ``` ::: ::: ## Occupancy estimates ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` y.1 y.2 y.3 y.4 psi.unconditional.Predicted psi.unconditional.SE 1 0 0 0 0 0 0.01 2 0 0 0 0 0 0.01 3 0 0 0 0 0 0.01 4 0 0 0 0 0 0.01 5 0 0 0 0 0 0.01 6 0 0 0 0 0 0.01 7 0 0 0 0 0 0.01 8 0 0 0 0 0 0.01 9 0 0 0 0 0 0.01 10 0 0 0 0 0 0.01 11 0 0 0 0 0 0.01 12 0 0 0 0 0 0.01 13 0 0 0 0 0 0.01 14 0 0 0 0 0 0.01 15 0 0 0 0 0 0.01 16 0 0 0 0 0 0.01 17 0 0 0 0 0 0.01 18 0 0 0 0 0 0.01 19 0 0 0 0 0 0.01 20 0 0 0 0 0 0.01 psi.unconditional.lower psi.unconditional.upper psi.conditional 1 0 1 0 2 0 1 0 3 0 1 0 4 0 1 0 5 0 1 0 6 0 1 0 7 0 1 0 8 0 1 0 9 0 1 0 10 0 1 0 11 0 1 0 12 0 1 0 13 0 1 0 14 0 1 0 15 0 1 0 16 0 1 0 17 0 1 0 18 0 1 0 19 0 1 0 20 0 1 0 ``` ::: ::: ## Occupancy estimates How many sites were occupied? We can answer this using posterior prediction. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} nsim <- 1000 sites.occupied.post <- predict(z.post, func=sum, nsim=nsim) par(mai=c(0.9,0.9,0.1,0.1)) plot(table(sites.occupied.post)/nsim, lwd=5, xlab="Sites occupied", ylab="Empirical Bayes posterior probability") abline(v=sum(z), col="red") ## Actual number occupied ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-occupancyI_files/figure-revealjs/bup-hist-1.png){fig-align='center' width=70%} ::: ::: ## Occupancy estimates The posterior median (or mean or mode) can be used as a point estimate: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} psi.cond.estimate <- median(sites.occupied.post) psi.cond.estimate ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0 ``` ::: ::: Quantiles can be used for the 95\% confidence interval: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} quantile(sites.occupied.post, prob=c(0.025, 0.975)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2.5% 97.5% 0 0 ``` ::: ::: ## Bayesian methods Bayesian methods incorporate prior distributions into inferences. We often have prior information, and it's easy to use. If we don't have prior information, we can use vague priors and obtain similar inferences as likelihood-based methods. Ultimately, we want the posterior distribution of the model parameters. We'll use MCMC to obtain samples from this distribution. ## JAGS and the jagsUI package A reminder... The basic steps of a Bayesian analysis with JAGS are: * Write a model in the BUGS language in a text file * Put data in a named list * Create a function to generate random initial values * Specify the parameters you want to monitor * Use MCMC to draw posterior samples * Use posterior samples for inference and prediction ## The BUGS language The BUGS model file: `occupancy-model.jag` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} writeLines(readLines("occupancy-model.jag")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` model { psi ~ dunif(0,1) # Prior for occupancy parameter p ~ dunif(0,1) # Prior for detection probability for(i in 1:nSites) { z[i] ~ dbern(psi) # Latent presence/absence for(j in 1:nOccasions) { y[i,j] ~ dbern(z[i]*p) # Model for the data } } sitesOccupied <- sum(z) # Total number of sites occupied } ``` ::: ::: ## Data, inits, and parameters Put data in a named list ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} jags.data <- list(y=y, nSites=nSites, nOccasions=nVisits) ``` :::
Initial values ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} jags.inits <- function() { list(psi=runif(1), p=runif(1), z=rep(1, nSites)) } ``` :::
Parameters to monitor ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} jags.pars <- c("psi", "p", "sitesOccupied") ``` ::: ## MCMC This function will compile the model, run adaptive MCMC, and then draw posterior samples using 3 Markov chains run in parallel. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## install.packages("jagsUI") library(jagsUI) jags.post.samples <- jags.basic(data=jags.data, inits=jags.inits, parameters.to.save=jags.pars, model.file="occupancy-model.jag", n.chains=3, n.adapt=100, n.burnin=0, n.iter=2000, parallel=TRUE) ``` ::: ## Summarize output ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(jags.post.samples[,1:4]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Iterations = 101:2100 Thinning interval = 1 Number of chains = 3 Sample size per chain = 2000 1. Empirical mean and standard deviation for each variable, plus standard error of the mean: Mean SD Naive SE Time-series SE deviance 0.8324 1.5492 0.020000 0.04832 p 0.3118 0.3093 0.003993 0.01293 psi 0.1603 0.2100 0.002711 0.01583 sitesOccupied 2.5653 4.4207 0.057072 0.33810 2. Quantiles for each variable: 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% deviance 0.000000 0.00000 0.0000 1.0588 5.3920 p 0.002431 0.03926 0.1851 0.5617 0.9517 psi 0.001886 0.02606 0.0693 0.2002 0.7902 sitesOccupied 0.000000 0.00000 0.0000 3.0000 16.0000 ``` ::: ::: ## Traceplots and density plots ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(jags.post.samples[,1:4]) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-occupancyI_files/figure-revealjs/bugs-plot-1.png){fig-align='center' width=70%} ::: ::: # Assignment {visibility="hidden"} ## Assignment ::: {style="font-size: 70%;"} Create a self-contained R script or Rmarkdown file to do the following: - Import the Canada Warbler data (`"cawa_data_2017_occu.csv"`) and compute basic summary stats like we did earlier. * Data are "point count data" from North Carolina * Each 10-min survey was divided into 4, 2.5-min intervals - Fit the single-season (static) occupancy model using 'unmarked' and 'JAGS'. - Create a `data.frame` to compare the estimates of $\psi$, $p$, and "nSitesOccupied" from the two analyses. Compare point estimates and 95\% CIs. Describe any differences you see in the estimates. :::
Upload your `.R` or `.Rmd` file to ELC by 5:00pm on Monday.

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
